mcqs.question: What single property of a feasibility check feasible(x) is required for binary search on the answer to be valid?
options: feasible(x) must run in O(1) time
feasible(x) must return true for at least half of all possible x values
The candidate answer range must contain fewer than 1000 values
Once feasible(x) becomes true (or false) at some value, it must stay that way for every larger value — monotonicity
mcqs.explanation: Monotonicity is the entire foundation of the technique — without a guarantee that feasibility only moves in one direction as x increases, there's no single boundary for binary search to converge on. The check's runtime cost, the fraction of true values, and the range size don't determine whether the technique is valid, only how efficient the overall search is.

mcqs.question: In the minimum-eating-speed problem, why is hours_needed(speed) <= h a valid feasibility check to binary search over?
options: Because hours_needed is always exactly equal to h at the true answer
Because a faster eating speed can only finish in the same time or less — never more — making feasibility monotonic as speed increases
Because the piles array is always sorted
Because hours_needed runs in constant time regardless of speed
mcqs.explanation: Increasing the eating speed can never increase the total hours needed — it either stays the same or decreases, which is exactly the monotonic relationship binary search on the answer requires. The piles array's sort order and the check's runtime cost are unrelated to why this specific check is valid to binary search over.

mcqs.question: In the ship-within-days problem, why does the search start with lo = max(weights) rather than lo = 1 or lo = 0?
options: Starting at max(weights) makes the search run faster but isn't required for correctness
lo = 1 would cause an infinite loop in this specific problem
Any capacity smaller than the single heaviest item can never be feasible at all, since that item alone wouldn't fit — so max(weights) is a provably valid lower bound
The weights array must be sorted before this bound is valid
mcqs.explanation: A ship capacity below the heaviest individual item literally cannot carry that item at all, making every capacity below max(weights) provably infeasible — starting there is a correctness requirement, ensuring the search's bounds actually contain the true answer, not just a speed optimization. There's no infinite-loop risk from a lower starting bound, and the weights array's sort order doesn't factor into this specific bound choice.

mcqs.question: If the initial [lo, hi] bounds for binary search on the answer don't actually contain the true answer, what happens?
options: The search throws a clear error indicating the bounds are invalid
The search runs to completion and returns some value within the given bounds — just not the correct answer, with nothing signaling the mistake
The search automatically expands lo and hi until the true answer is included
The search always returns exactly lo or exactly hi in this case
mcqs.explanation: Binary search has no way to know its bounds are wrong — it will converge on some value within [lo, hi] and terminate normally, silently returning an incorrect result with no error or signal that anything went wrong. There's no automatic bounds expansion, and the returned value isn't necessarily exactly lo or hi — it converges to whatever boundary the feasibility check produces within the given (wrong) range.

mcqs.question: When binary searching over a range of real numbers (rather than integers) to some required precision, what must change about the loop's termination condition?
options: The feasibility check itself must be rewritten entirely for real numbers
Nothing changes — while lo < hi works identically for real numbers
The loop should instead run a fixed number of iterations or use a tolerance check (hi - lo > epsilon), since real numbers have no 'next' value the way integers do for lo == hi to trigger
Real-number binary search is not possible and requires a completely different algorithm
mcqs.explanation: Integers have a well-defined next value, so lo == hi is a meaningful stopping point, but real numbers can be subdivided indefinitely — so termination has to be based on either a fixed iteration count or a small tolerance window instead. The feasibility-check logic itself is unchanged; only the loop's termination condition needs to adapt, and the pattern absolutely still applies to real numbers with this adjustment.

mcqs.question: A candidate applies binary search on the answer to a problem where feasible(x) is true, then false, then true again as x increases across the range. What happens?
options: Binary search still works correctly, just takes a few more iterations
The technique silently breaks — the search can converge on a boundary that isn't the actual answer, since it assumes a single clean transition that doesn't exist
The feasibility check will throw an exception when this pattern is detected
This situation is impossible for any real-world feasibility check
mcqs.explanation: Binary search on the answer fundamentally assumes exactly one transition point between infeasible and feasible — when the predicate isn't monotonic, the algorithm has no way to detect this and will converge on whichever boundary its comparisons happen to land near, which may not be the true answer at all. There's no exception thrown to signal the violation, and non-monotonic predicates are a real risk worth checking for, not an impossible edge case.
